Date: 2025-08-19

Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Daniel Cho (Redwood SE), Maya Thompson (GreenLoop Eng Mgr), Arjun Patel (GreenLoop ML Eng), Sophie Li (GreenLoop CTO)

Summary: quick hosted api live demo focusing on streaming behavior and retry strategies. Some audio glitches, auto-transcription errors present (product names occasionally garbled).

[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Lena from Redwood, this is Daniel our SE. How's every-- can you all hear okay?
[00:06] Maya: Yep good here. Thanks.
[00:08] Sophie: All good.
[00:10] Lena: Great. Quick agenda: we'll do a short intro, then Daniel will share his screen and walk the hosted streaming path, show param tuning, streaming chunks, and then we'll cover retries/backoff and what that looks like from the console. We'll leave time for Qs.
[00:23] Daniel: Alright I'm sharing. Can you see my browser — console, request inspector?
[00:28] Arjun: Yup seeing it. The console looks slick.
[00:31] Daniel: Cool — first thing: streaming in the hosted API is chunked. It's not one big monolithic response, it emits incremental deltas as tokens are produced. That lets you pipe partial outputs to the UI to reduce perceived latency.
[00:43] Maya: Is that server-sent events or websockets under the hood?
[00:46] Daniel: Mostly Server-Sent Events (SSE) for text streaming over HTTP/1.1; SDKs wrap it and provide websocket-like callbacks. There are slight differences with our JS/py SDKs but semantics are the same: you get ordered deltas.
[00:58] Sophie: Any recomposition issues if a chunk drops?
[01:01] Daniel: Good question. Chunks are stateless deltas — if a chunk is lost you might see a small gap. The client SDK will re-request the tail with the cached prefix depending on idempotency. For critical flows we recommend you enable prefix caching and idempotency tokens so you can safely retry without duplicating side effects.
[01:18] Lena: We do have customers that stream to UIs so preserving order matters. Also our console shows token-level timing so you can see where tail latency is coming from.
[01:27] Arjun: You mentioned prefix caching — that’s the K V cache thing we saw in the docs? I think it said KV cache.
[01:31] Daniel: Yeah K-V cache, sorry auto-transcript spells it differently sometimes. The idea: if you're chatting and you retransmit a previous prefix, the runtime can reuse cached keys for the prefix to avoid re-computing attention for the whole sequence which speeds up retries.
[01:45] Maya: Walk us through params. We have a bunch of stuff in our frontend — temperature, top_p, max_tokens. Defaults are a bit fuzzy in our app.
[01:52] Daniel: On hosted we set conservative defaults: temperature 0.8, top_p 0.95, and max_tokens default to 256 for chat endpoints. But for deterministic assistant flows we often set temp 0.0–0.3 and top_p 0.8. Also you can control stream_chunk_size in the SDK — smaller chunk size means more frequent partials but higher overhead.
[02:13] Sophie: How does stream_chunk_size interact with latency? If we set very small chunks will that increase latency because of overhead?
[02:18] Daniel: Exactly — there's a sweet spot. Small chunk sizes reduce first-byte latency on the UI but increase per-chunk processing overhead and potentially network overhead. Our runtime aggregates tokens efficiently but for high throughput clients we recommend chunk sizes around 8–16 tokens. We'll bench with your prompts to recommend values.
[02:34] Maya: Can you demo a retry? We had an incident where 2% of streaming sessions aborted mid-stream and the frontend had to show an error.
[02:41] Daniel: Sure. I'll simulate a transient connection drop from the client.
[02:45] [screen action: Daniel toggles network emulator — simulating socket reset]
[02:50] Daniel: You see that the SDK automatically attempts to reconnect and then replays from the last acknowledged token when idempotency is on. If you don't set idempotency token, the server treats it as a new request and you'll get a new generation.
[03:05] Arjun: So for us, we need no duplicates — our downstream cannot accept duplicate side effects. Is idempotency token enough?
[03:11] Daniel: If you need strict no-duplicates, combine idempotency tokens with server-side request markers (we support a request metadata header) and avoid non-idempotent side effects in prompts. For example, if the model triggers external calls, isolate those on your backend after the model response is finalized.
[03:27] Lena: Also worth noting: retries are best-effort. For longer generations, if the streaming window exceeds retention thresholds we fall back to server-side cached variant or a synchronous re-generation. We show this in the console as a reroute event.
[03:40] Maya: What's the recommended backoff strategy?
[03:42] Daniel: Exponential backoff with jitter. We recommend initial retry after 250–500ms for transient connection resets, double each time, cap at 8–10s, and give up after 3 attempts by default. Our SDKs have built-in retry policies you can configure.
[03:57] Sophie: And what about idempotency TTL? How long do tokens last on the server?
[04:01] Daniel: By default idempotency metadata is persisted for 24 hours; for Dedicated contracts we can extend retention if you need longer windows.
[04:09] Arjun: If we do a reconnect and re-request the last 200 tokens, does the server reuse the KV cache or will it recompute?
[04:16] Daniel: If the KV cache for that prefix is still warm, the runtime will reuse it; otherwise there’s a short recompute penalty. That's why we recommend sticky routing for low-latency use cases.
[04:25] [05:00] Daniel: Switching to the console — here’s a live request inspector. You can see per-token timing, token counts, estimated cost, and which model variant served the request.
[05:12] Maya: That's helpful. I see a column labeled "approx cost" — is that actual billing?
[05:16] Lena: It's an estimate for quick troubleshooting. Billing will be slightly different because of rounding and aggregation but it tracks closely.
[05:22] Daniel: Another quick note on retries and duplicates: for chat flows where you append state server-side, the recommended pattern is to buffer generated deltas client-side until the stream completes or until you confirm with an end-of-stream sentinel, then persist. That avoids partial-side-effect writes.
[05:40] Arjun: Do you provide server-side hooks for function-calling so we can see partial tool-invocation intents?
[05:45] Daniel: Yes — we stream function call deltas as structured JSON chunks; sometimes transcriptions show those as weird tokens in the transcript. The SDK will raise a function-call event when enough structured data is available.
[05:58] Maya: We have a heavy fan-out to real-time personalization — lots of short prompts, many concurrent sessions. Would hosted hit concurrency limits?
[06:05] Lena: Hosted has soft concurrency quotas per account; if you expect very sustained high concurrency we usually recommend Dedicated or burst agreements. Dedicated gives you guaranteed slots and reduced tail latencies.
[06:18] Sophie: If we go Dedicated, does the API surface change much?
[06:21] Daniel: Very minimal — same endpoints and SDKs, mostly different routing and capacity guarantees. You still get console observability either way.
[06:30] Maya: Any best practices for temperature and top_p for our use case — short personalization prompts where hallucination low tolerance?
[06:36] Daniel: Keep temperature low 0.0–0.2 and top_p 0.7–0.9. Also consider nucleus sampling vs deterministic beam-style outputs via constrained decoding — Redwood supports stop token lists and token biasing to reduce degenerate outputs.
[06:52] Arjun: About partial transcripts — our frontend relies on partials to show streaming suggestions. If a chunk is delayed, is there a reordering risk?
[06:57] Daniel: No reordering risk — chunks are ordered at the event stream layer. Delays can make parts arrive late but the sequence is preserved.
[07:04] Maya: You mentioned automatic fallback to smaller model or cached variant under load — can you explain?
[07:08] Daniel: Our routing policy can shift to a lower-cost or quantized variant when latency SLOs can't be met. It tries compatible variants first. The console flags the fallback and you can set A/B policies to control automatic fallbacks.
[07:20] Sophie: Would that change output quality in a way that breaks UX?
[07:23] Daniel: Potentially; that's why we add quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. Redwood Optimize can suggest quantization profiles and flag prompt regressions.
[07:33] Maya: Any gotchas around streaming with proxies or CDNs?
[07:37] Daniel: Proxies that buffer responses (some corporate proxies) will break SSE streaming semantics. For production we recommend bypassing buffering via direct connections or using websockets where SSE isn't supported.
[07:49] Arjun: Last technical Q: For retries, are there any idempotency header names we should use?
[07:54] Daniel: Use X-Redwood-Idempotency-Key or the SDK helper that sets it for you. Also include X-Request-Metadata for tracing and connect it to your internal request ID.
[08:05] Lena: Ok quick 3-min wrap and next steps. We'll run a perf bench, send pricing and security docs, and reconvene for results.
[08:12] Maya: Sounds good, thanks both.
[08:14] Sophie: Thanks, that was useful.
